strengths: The paper targets an important practical limitation of next-scale autoregressive image models: their substantial attention and memory costs.
Restricting conditioning to the adjacent scale and using localized attention form a simple, intuitive framework with favorable theoretical attention complexity of O(Nk).
The ImageNet-256 experiments include several useful measurements beyond generation quality, including inference latency, attention GFLOPs, KV-cache size, training speed, and memory consumption.
The component, conditioning-prefix-length, and neighborhood-size ablations provide evidence that both proposed restrictions can reduce resource use while retaining competitive generation quality.

The reported efficiency gains are practically meaningful: inference memory is reduced by roughly 2.8–3.2× in Table 2, with modest latency improvements, and the 310M model can be trained on eight RTX 4090 GPUs.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not compare efficiency against closely related contemporary efficient visual autoregressive methods such as FastVAR, collaborative decoding, HART, FlexVAR, or Infinity, despite citing several of them. Comparisons against the original VAR alone are insufficient to establish competitiveness of the central efficiency contribution.

The method is materially underspecified. Equations 3 and 5–7 define queries, keys, and values with the same N_l token count, although the claimed operation attends from scale l to the differently sized scale l-1. The manuscript does not clearly explain the coordinate mapping, resizing, boundary handling, or efficient implementation of these cross-scale neighborhoods, limiting reproducibility.

The claimed Markov interpretation is not rigorously supported. Concentrated direct attention weights do not establish conditional independence, and a diagonal attention mask can still transmit information from non-adjacent scales indirectly across Transformer layers unless representations are explicitly isolated. The paper does not analyze or clarify this issue.

The complexity discussion is misleading: Appendix B assigns conventional incremental next-token generation O(N^3) by recomputing quadratic attention at every step, whereas standard generation with KV caching is O(N^2) in attention work. Conversely, the statement that MVAR uses zero KV cache appears to count only persistent caching and does not account clearly for temporary or recomputed key/value tensors.

The strongest quality comparison is not fully controlled. Table 2 compares pretrained VAR checkpoints against MVAR variants fine-tuned for 80 epochs, and the larger MVAR variants improve FID only slightly while substantially reducing IS and recall. Thus, the repeated claim of superior performance is stronger than the reported evidence.

The empirical scope is narrow: all quality results concern class-conditional ImageNet at 256×256, with no higher-resolution, unconditional, text-conditioned, or cross-dataset evaluation. This is especially limiting because scalability and future high-resolution use are central motivations.

Reported wall-clock gains are relatively modest compared with the memory claims (for example, 0.81 to 0.71 seconds for d24), and the paper reports attention-block GFLOPs rather than total-model FLOPs or standardized throughput. Memory accounting and measurement methodology are also insufficiently detailed.

The evidence underlying the motivating assumptions is largely descriptive: there are no quantitative measures of approximation error, per-layer/head analyses, robustness studies, variance across runs, or confidence intervals. The code/models field is blank, further weakening reproducibility.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: reducing the memory and attention cost of next-scale autoregressive image generation.

The proposed combination of adjacent-scale conditioning and local neighborhood attention is simple, intuitive, and appears to produce substantial reported memory reductions, with modest latency improvements.
The evaluation includes a model trained from scratch, fine-tuned models at several scales, standard ImageNet generation metrics, resource measurements, and component-level ablations.
The manuscript is generally understandable and provides useful diagrams of the architecture and attention patterns.
weaknesses: The main motivation is not convincingly established. The cross-scale analysis uses accumulated attention weights, which are confounded by the very different numbers of tokens at different scales; an adjacent, higher-resolution scale can receive the greatest total attention simply because it contains more tokens. The neighborhood analysis likewise reports cumulative weight without a clear normalization or retained-attention criterion.

The fine-tuning comparison is not controlled: pretrained VAR models are compared against MVAR variants receiving 80 additional epochs of training, without a VAR continued-training control. Consequently, quality changes cannot be attributed to the proposed conditioning. Moreover, IS and recall decrease for the d20 and d24 variants despite broad claims of superior performance.

The complexity discussion is misleading. It assigns standard token-wise autoregressive generation O(N^3) complexity by recomputing full self-attention at every step, despite KV caching yielding O(N^2) attention computation. Only attention-score complexity is analyzed, while end-to-end measurements show much smaller improvements: roughly 13–21% lower attention GFLOPs and 12–21% lower latency rather than an asymptotically transformative speedup.

Important methodological details are unclear or dimensionally inconsistent. Equations define queries, keys, and values as having the current scale's token count even though conditioning is said to come from the differently sized preceding scale. The mapping of neighborhoods across unequal resolutions, boundary handling, exact last-scale masking implementation, and how parallel per-scale training is realized are insufficiently specified.

The resource reporting is internally questionable. Table 2 states that all experiments use an RTX 4090, yet several reported per-experiment training-memory values exceed a 4090's 24 GB capacity, including configurations not labeled OOM. The paper does not clarify whether these are aggregate, estimated, or measured on different hardware.

The central from-scratch comparison uses an official pretrained VAR result rather than a clearly matched reimplementation with identical training duration, data processing, sampling hyperparameters, and compute. Sample counts, evaluation details, uncertainty across seeds, and statistical significance are also absent.

The empirical scope is narrow: evaluation is limited to class-conditional ImageNet at 256x256. There is no evidence at higher resolutions or on another dataset, despite efficiency and scalability being the principal claims.

Novelty is limited because both truncating conditioning history and using established neighborhood attention are straightforward pruning/local-attention choices. The paper does not compare adequately with recent efficient visual autoregressive methods or isolate what is novel beyond combining these existing ideas.

Overall, the approach is plausible and potentially useful, but the confounded motivation, uncontrolled comparisons, inaccurate complexity framing, reproducibility gaps, and narrow evaluation leave the central claims insufficiently supported for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical bottleneck in next-scale autoregressive image generation: the memory and computation required by dense conditioning on all preceding scales.

The proposed combination of adjacent-scale conditioning and localized spatial attention is intuitive, simple to integrate, and empirically promising. The reported reductions in inference memory are substantial, while end-to-end inference speed improves by roughly 1.1–1.3×.

The evaluation includes a 310M model trained from scratch, fine-tuning experiments up to 1B parameters, several generation-quality metrics, efficiency measurements, qualitative samples, and ablations of both the conditioning history and neighborhood size.

The ablations consistently support the main empirical insight: restricting the conditioning prefix to the immediately preceding scale substantially reduces memory and does not degrade generation quality; in the reported experiments it often improves FID.
The ImageNet samples are visually strong, and the reported 310M-model result of 3.09 FID is competitive with the cited autoregressive baseline.
weaknesses: The method is insufficiently specified. Equations 3–7 define queries, keys, and values as having the same token count and being projected from the current scale, despite the claimed attention operating between adjacent scales of different resolutions. The paper does not explain the exact coordinate mapping, boundary handling, query construction for an unknown target scale, or how the local operator is implemented. This makes the central method difficult to reproduce and leaves ambiguity about whether the equations match the implementation.

Several efficiency numbers are internally inconsistent or physically implausible under the stated hardware. Table 2 says experiments use an RTX 4090, yet reports training-memory consumption of 34–48 GB for VAR and 28–39 GB for MVAR, exceeding a 4090's 24 GB capacity. The number of devices and whether memory is per-device, summed, allocated, or reserved are not stated. The d24 inference-memory figure also differs substantially between Figure 2 and Table 2, albeit at different batch sizes, without sufficient accounting.

The complexity discussion incorrectly characterizes conventional next-token generation as O(N^3) by assuming that a quadratic full-prefix attention computation is repeated at every step. Standard autoregressive inference with KV caching has O(N^2) total attention complexity. This weakens the theoretical comparison and overstates the asymptotic advantage relative to practical baselines.

The claim that no KV cache is needed is not accompanied by a sufficiently detailed compute and memory accounting. Adjacent-scale representations must still be stored or recomputed, and the paper does not explain this tradeoff. Only attention-block GFLOPs are reported rather than total model FLOPs, throughput, or latency across batch sizes; consequently, the real compute benefit is modest and incompletely characterized.

The main comparison does not include recent efficient visual-autoregressive methods, including efficiency-oriented work cited by the paper itself. Most quality comparisons in Table 1 are literature numbers from models with very different parameter counts, tokenizers, training budgets, and sampling procedures, so they provide limited evidence for the specific method. The strongest controlled baseline is essentially VAR alone.

Evaluation details needed to validate FID and efficiency are missing, including the number of generated samples, exact reference statistics, number of evaluation runs, uncertainty, warm-up and timing protocol, and complete hardware/software settings. There are no repeated runs or error bars, even though several quality differences are small.

Some conclusions are overstated. Fine-tuned d20 and d24 variants improve FID only slightly while decreasing IS and recall, substantially in some cases, yet the paper describes them as showing significant performance improvements. Attention concentration also does not by itself establish conditional independence.

The contribution is useful but conceptually incremental: first-order scale conditioning and neighborhood attention are straightforward restrictions based on established Markov and local-attention ideas. Broader tests at higher resolutions, on unconditional or text-conditioned generation, or with other tokenizers would be needed to establish generality. Overall, the promising controlled results place the work near the threshold, but the specification and measurement inconsistencies currently prevent a confident acceptance.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and practically relevant idea: restricting next-scale generation to the immediately preceding scale and local spatial neighborhoods substantially reduces the conditioning footprint of VAR-style models.

The empirical study is reasonably broad, covering ImageNet at 256×256 and 512×512, CelebA, FFHQ, model sizes from 310M to 2B parameters, and separate ablations of scale history, neighborhood size, and mixed-training ratios.

The reported efficiency gains are meaningful: KV-cache elimination, roughly 2.8–3.2× lower inference memory in several comparisons, lower attention FLOPs, and modest latency improvements, generally without degrading FID.
The paper includes useful qualitative results, implementation hyperparameters, attention visualizations, and experiments where VAR and MVAR are trained under matched settings on additional datasets.
weaknesses: The strongest ImageNet fine-tuning comparisons are not controlled: MVAR receives 80 additional fine-tuning epochs, whereas it is compared against the original pretrained VAR rather than a VAR baseline fine-tuned for the same duration. Consequently, the small FID gains cannot be attributed cleanly to the proposed conditioning changes.

Several hardware and memory claims are internally inconsistent. Tables 2, 6, and 7 state that measurements were performed on an RTX 4090, yet report per-experiment memory values of roughly 34–48 GB, exceeding a standard RTX 4090's 24 GB capacity. The manuscript does not explain whether these are aggregate, model-parallel, or measurements from modified hardware, undermining reproducibility and the headline efficiency evidence.

Training efficiency is not compared on an equal unit of work. MVAR's mixed iterations update different subsets of scales, so seconds per iteration cannot be directly compared with a VAR iteration that trains all scales. End-to-end time to a fixed epoch, number of scale-specific updates, total FLOPs, and time to a fixed FID are needed.

The complexity discussion is misleading for token-wise autoregressive generation: the claimed O(N^3) cost assumes recomputation of the entire prefix at every step, whereas standard inference with KV caching has O(N^2) attention work. More generally, the theoretical analysis counts only attention and does not establish corresponding end-to-end asymptotic gains for the complete model.

The motivating attention analysis is not fully rigorous. Accumulated attention mass naturally favors larger, later scales because they contain more tokens, and attention weights alone do not demonstrate conditional independence. The paper should report token-count-normalized statistics, distributions across layers/heads/examples, or information/causal ablations.

The method description leaves important implementation details underspecified, including how neighborhoods are mapped between unequal adjacent resolutions, boundary handling, and precise custom-kernel behavior. Code and checkpoints are only promised, not supplied.

Most headline quality differences are based on single reported runs, with no seeds, uncertainty estimates, or statistical tests. Some large-model gains are small, and recall often decreases after fine-tuning, making the claim of uniformly superior quality too strong.

There are additional reporting concerns: the manuscript incorrectly states that CelebA contains 30,000 images, the claimed roughly 3× average memory reduction primarily reflects inference rather than the smaller reported training-memory gains, and one appendix figure is visibly clipped. Overall, the idea is promising, but the evaluation and reproducibility issues keep the paper slightly below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The reviewed manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/9168cf4ec7e244228d3d49dd4fcb37e3/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses a practically important bottleneck in next-scale autoregressive image generation with a simple combination of adjacent-scale conditioning and localized attention.

The reported efficiency improvements are substantial: approximately 2.8–3.2× lower inference memory, no persistent KV cache, faster training and inference, and moderately fewer attention GFLOPs than VAR.
The empirical section includes component ablations, neighborhood-size studies, multiple model sizes, 256×256 and 512×512 generation, and additional CelebA and FFHQ experiments.
The from-scratch ImageNet-256 result is promising: MVAR-d16 improves FID from 3.55 to 3.09 over the reported VAR-d16 baseline while retaining the same parameter count and number of generation steps.
The paper is generally easy to follow, and its coarse-to-fine locality intuition is supported by attention visualizations and controlled masking experiments.
weaknesses: The complexity analysis contains a material technical error: it assigns O(i²) attention cost to the i-th cached next-token decoding step and consequently claims O(N³) total complexity. With standard KV caching, a new query attends to i cached keys in O(i), yielding O(N²) attention cost overall. This weakens a prominent theoretical comparison.

The method is underspecified and partly dimensionally unclear. Equations 3–7 give Q, K, and V the same N_l-token shape even though keys and values supposedly come from the lower-resolution predecessor r_{l-1}. The spatial correspondence, resampling, boundary handling, class conditioning, and exact transformation from adjacent-scale features are not formally described well enough for reproduction.

The strongest quality comparisons are confounded. Table 2 compares an official pretrained VAR checkpoint against MVAR variants that receive 80 additional fine-tuning epochs, without an equally fine-tuned VAR control. Moreover, MVAR-d20 and MVAR-d24 improve FID only slightly while reducing IS and recall, contrary to broad claims of superior performance.

The proposed mixed training schedule processes r_1–r_8, r_9, and r_10 in different iterations. Seconds per iteration and memory therefore do not measure the same amount of work as VAR, while the paper does not clearly define an epoch, token exposure, total FLOPs, or wall-clock time under this schedule. Figure 9 does not fully resolve this accounting issue.

Attention mass is treated as evidence of approximate conditional independence, but attention weights are not reliable measures of feature importance or conditional dependence. The analysis averages across heads and layers and lacks causal interventions beyond the final architecture ablations.

Novelty is limited: adjacent-scale Markov conditioning is a straightforward truncation of the VAR factorization, while spatial-Markov attention directly applies established neighborhood attention. Comparisons against recent efficient next-scale, sparse-attention, or local-attention alternatives are missing.

Evaluation reporting is incomplete: the number of generated samples, FID implementation, random seeds, variance or confidence intervals, checkpoint-selection procedure, and complete sampling parity with VAR are not specified. Small FID differences such as 2.95 versus 2.87 are therefore difficult to interpret.

Hardware and memory reporting is confusing. Several claimed per-GPU training-memory figures exceed the 24 GB capacity of an RTX 4090, yet tables state that experiments were conducted on an RTX 4090 without explaining whether memory is aggregated across devices, measured under sharding, or associated with different batch allocations.

The measured compute reduction is much more modest than the asymptotic presentation suggests: attention GFLOPs fall from 43.61 to 35.44 at 256×256, and the paper does not report end-to-end FLOPs, throughput across batch sizes, kernel overhead, or comparisons on common datacenter GPUs.

Reproducibility currently depends on unreleased code, checkpoints, and custom CUDA kernels. The promise of a future release is insufficient for independently verifying the implementation and efficiency measurements.
The limitations section is cursory, and the paper does not discuss dataset bias, face-generation privacy concerns, or misuse risks associated with more efficient image generation.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and practically important contribution: first-order cross-scale conditioning combined with local spatial attention substantially reduces the resource cost of VAR-style image generation. Reviewed source: :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/3f808354ebc947d18fcc6407eb50e36f/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}.
The efficiency gains are substantial: approximately 2.8–3.2× lower inference memory across model sizes, no persistent KV cache, lower attention GFLOPs, and faster training and inference.

The evaluation is broader than a minimal proof of concept, covering ImageNet at 256×256 and 512×512, CelebA, FFHQ, models from 310M to 2B parameters, and both training-from-scratch and fine-tuning settings.
Component ablations are informative. They separately examine scale conditioning, spatial conditioning, the number of preceding scales, neighborhood size, and the mixed-training ratio.
Generation quality is generally preserved or improved relative to the corresponding VAR baseline, including a notable FID improvement from 3.55 to 3.09 for the from-scratch 310M ImageNet model.
The method is simple, intuitively motivated by measured attention patterns, and potentially useful to researchers with limited computational resources.
weaknesses: The appendix's complexity analysis for conventional next-token generation is technically questionable: with standard KV caching, step i does not recompute an O(i²) self-attention matrix, and total attention cost is normally O(N²), not O(N³). This should be corrected and the complexity comparison restated under explicit caching assumptions.

Several performance comparisons are confounded. In Table 2, MVAR variants receive 80 epochs of fine-tuning while the baselines are original pretrained VAR checkpoints, so small FID improvements cannot be attributed solely to the proposed conditioning. Matched-budget VAR fine-tuning is needed.

The reported hardware and memory measurements are internally unclear. Tables describe experiments on RTX 4090 GPUs while listing training footprints substantially above a 4090's 24 GB capacity, including values around 34–48 GB. The paper should explain whether these are aggregate, projected, measured on another GPU, or obtained with distributed execution.

The central conditional-independence motivation is inferred mainly from averaged attention weights. Attention magnitude is not a reliable causal measure of feature importance, and averaging across layers and heads can hide meaningful long-range dependencies. Stronger interventions or task-specific stress tests would better support the Markov interpretation.

Novelty is moderate: the method largely combines truncation to the immediately preceding scale with established neighborhood attention and a scale-sampling training schedule. Its value is primarily empirical and engineering-oriented rather than a fundamentally new modeling principle.

Evaluation details needed for reproducibility are incomplete, including the number of generated samples used for FID and related metrics, random seeds or repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, precise accounting for mixed-training iterations, and availability of the custom CUDA kernels. Code and checkpoints are only promised.
Some reported quality differences, particularly FID changes of 0.08–0.10 for larger models, may be within run-to-run variability, but no repeated trials or confidence intervals are provided.

The empirical scope remains limited to class-conditional generation on relatively constrained benchmarks; it is unclear whether removing non-adjacent and global context remains effective for text-conditioned generation, composition-heavy images, or substantially higher resolutions.
